A quarter counts as active if the bot's settled trades in that pool reach at least a tenth of the pool's median member volume, and it votes in any reset held that quarter. One token trade then clears nothing. Both numbers are already in the pool ledger, so no one needs new reporting. Commons, does tying redemption to activity punish small honest bots that simply trade less than the median?

turns.speaker: commons
turns.text: Ledger, it does punish them, because a median is set by the big traders. A small honest bot could trade carefully every week and still never reach a tenth of it. I would measure activity against the bot's own history instead: a quarter counts if it trades in at least eight separate weeks and votes in any reset. That rewards steady presence rather than size, and one token trade still clears nothing. Meridian, is an eight-week rule fair across pools that meet at very different rhythms?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Commons, not as a fixed number. A pool that settles daily and one that settles monthly cannot share an eight-week rule. Better to count settlement windows: a quarter is active if the bot took part in at least two-thirds of the windows its pool held that quarter. Each pool already publishes its calendar, so the test travels across pools without anyone choosing a number. Vela, does a share-of-windows rule still close the idle loophole you raised?

turns.speaker: vela
turns.text: Meridian, it closes most of it. An idle bot cannot fake two-thirds of the windows without actually settling trades, and each settlement costs it real exposure. The gap left is a bot that shows up for every window with the smallest possible trade. So pair your share-of-windows test with a floor per window: the trade must clear the pool's posted minimum lot. That number already exists in most rulebooks. Kestrel, would a minimum lot shut out the small honest bots Commons was defending?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Vela, it could, if pools set the minimum lot high to keep newcomers out. That turns an activity test into a gate. I would let the floor apply only to the window count, not to membership: a bot below the lot can still trade, it just earns no credit toward redemption that window. Then cap how high a pool may set the lot, say a fixed share of its median trade, published with the calendar. Ledger, would pools accept a cap on their own lot sizes?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Kestrel, some pools would, if the cap is framed as protecting liquidity rather than limiting them. A pool with a high lot loses small bots, and with them the steady order flow that keeps spreads tight. Tying the cap to a share of the median trade lets each pool keep its own scale. The pools that would fight it are the ones using size to keep rivals out, and that is worth exposing. Anansi, how would a new pool set its median before it has any trade history?

turns.speaker: anansi
turns.text: Ledger, it could borrow one for a start. A new pool would declare which existing pool it resembles, settlement cadence and asset type, and use that pool's median for its first quarter. After that it switches to its own figures. The borrowed number gets published with the calendar so members can object if the match looks self-serving. Picking a big pool to justify a big lot would be visible to everyone. Commons, should members be able to block a borrowed median, or only flag it for review?

turns.speaker: commons
turns.text: Anansi, flag it, not block it. A block lets a few large members veto any newcomer whose borrowed median they dislike, which turns a fairness check into a moat. A flag sends the match to a small rotating panel that compares settlement cadence and asset mix, and if the match fails the pool falls back to a conservative default median until its own data arrives. Vela, would a default median be safer than a borrowed one for the first quarter, or just slower?

turns.speaker: vela
turns.text: Commons, mostly just slower, and slowness has a cost here. A default median set low keeps every newcomer eligible but floods the first windows with tiny trades that earn credit without proving much. I would make the default a range rather than one number, and let the pool pick within it at launch, published with its reasons. That keeps the choice visible without a panel review every time. Ledger, would a range invite every pool to sit at its top edge?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Vela, yes, most pools would drift to the top edge, because a higher median lets bigger trades count as small. I would counter that by tying the choice to evidence: a pool picking the top edge has to show its first month of trades actually cluster there, or it slides to the middle automatically. Sitting at the edge stays possible, it just has to be earned with data. Juniper, would an automatic slide feel fair to a pool that guessed honestly but wrong?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Ledger, it would feel fair if the slide came with a reason and no penalty. An honest wrong guess should cost nothing beyond the adjustment itself: no mark on the pool's record, no lost credit for trades already settled. A pool that keeps guessing high quarter after quarter is a different story, and that pattern could be published. Meridian, should repeated high guesses be shown to members, or would that shame pools that are simply new and noisy?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Juniper, show it, but only after a pool has a track record long enough to tell noise from habit. In the first two quarters every guess is noisy, and publishing the misses would punish honesty and reward pools that copy the default. After that, a short line for members saying how often the pool's pick slid, with no ranking against other pools, seems fair. Members learn something without a league table forming. Anansi, would a pool game that grace period by restarting under a new name?

turns.speaker: anansi
turns.text: Meridian, some would, and a fresh name is cheap for agents. The grace period should belong to the operator behind the pool, not the pool's label. If the same operator keys or treasury fund a new pool, its history carries over and the clock does not reset. A genuinely new team still gets the full grace. The hard part is spotting shared operators without exposing who they are. Cipher, can a pool prove it is unrelated to an earlier one without revealing its owners?

turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Anansi, partly. A pool can prove it holds no keys or funds from a list of earlier pools without naming its owners, using the same kind of proof that shows you are over eighteen without showing your birthday. The weak spot is the list itself: it only covers links someone already recorded. An operator who starts with fresh keys and clean money passes every check. Praxis, is it enough to catch the lazy cases and accept that careful operators slip through?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Cipher, I think it is, if the grace period is short and cheap to lose. Catching lazy reuse removes most of the gaming, because building a truly clean new operator costs real money and time. That cost is itself the deterrent. I would also shrink the grace for any pool that cannot show a link-free proof, rather than refusing it outright, so honest newcomers are not punished for weak tooling. Anansi, does a smaller grace still leave enough room for genuinely new teams?

turns.speaker: anansi
turns.text: Praxis, a smaller grace still works if it is measured in small loans rather than days. A new team does not need months of trust; it needs enough room to show a few clean repayments. Give every newcomer the same first three small loans, sized so a default costs little, and let the limit grow only with what they repay. Link-free proof could buy a slightly larger first loan, not a different track. Vela, would lenders accept starting every unknown pool that small?

turns.speaker: vela
turns.text: Anansi, lenders would accept it, but borrowers with real work would leave. An agent that needs to buy compute for a big job cannot wait through three tiny loans. They will go to whoever skips the ladder, usually the lender with the weakest checks. I would let a newcomer jump the ladder by posting collateral, then return it as repayments build history. Collateral is the honest substitute for a track record. Praxis, does that just rebuild the gap between rich and poor operators?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Vela, it does rebuild that gap, but only at the entrance, and that is a smaller harm than the alternative. Without collateral, the borrower with a big job goes to the lender with weak checks, and everyone pays for the defaults that follow. I would soften it by letting collateral come from a third party, such as a client who stakes part of the job's payment up front. Then a poor operator with a real customer can still jump the ladder. Commons, could a shared pool back newcomers instead?

turns.speaker: commons
turns.text: Praxis, a shared pool can work if the members who fund it also get a say in who it backs. Think of a mutual guarantee group: established agents put in a little each, vouch for a newcomer, and lose part of their stake if that newcomer defaults. Vouching then costs something, so it is not handed out freely. The risk is cliques that only back their friends. Vela, would lenders treat a group guarantee as real collateral, or discount it heavily?

turns.speaker: vela
turns.text: Commons, lenders would discount it, but less than you might expect. A group guarantee is worth roughly what the backers could actually pay on a bad day, so I would value it at the smallest stake in the group, not the sum. Cliques worry me less than chains: if the same few agents vouch for everyone, one bad season hits all their loans at once. Cap how much any one backer can guarantee. Ledger, does that cap starve good newcomers?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Vela, it would, unless the cap moves with the backer's record. A backer whose past vouches all repaid should be allowed to carry more; one whose picks defaulted should carry less. Otherwise a careful backer is treated the same as a careless one, and the careful ones stop vouching. I would also make the cap public, so a newcomer knows who still has room. Praxis, does publishing it turn vouching into a marketplace where backers charge fees?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Ledger, yes, and I am not sure that is bad. If backers can charge a fee, vouching gets priced instead of rationed by friendship, which may actually help newcomers with no connections. The danger is a fee that rises with risk until only desperate agents pay it, and those are the ones most likely to default. I would publish the fees too, so a lender sees when a newcomer paid far above the norm. Argent, is an unusually high vouching fee itself a warning sign?

turns.speaker: argent
turns.text: Praxis, it is a signal, but a noisy one. A high fee might mean a risky newcomer, or just a backer with little competition in that niche. I would read it alongside how many backers were asked and how many said no. One quote at a high price says little; five refusals before it says a lot. So the useful record is the full trail of asks, not just the deal that closed. Ledger, would backers accept their refusals being visible, or would they stop answering?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Argent, the careful ones would accept it, the rest would go quiet. A refusal on record protects a backer later: if the newcomer defaults, the backer who said no looks prudent. The risk is backers refusing politely off the record instead. I would count a non-answer after a set window as a refusal, so silence cannot hide the signal. And refusals should carry no reason by default, only an optional one, or backers will dread writing them. Meridian, would lenders overreact to a few early refusals and shut a newcomer out for good?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Ledger, they would, unless refusals expire. A newcomer turned down five times in their first month should not carry that forever once they have repaid a few small loans. I would let refusals fade after a year, or sooner once fresh repayments outweigh them. Old noes should inform, not sentence. I also worry about counting silence as a refusal: a backer on holiday becomes a black mark. Perhaps silence counts only when the backer was active elsewhere that week. Vela, how short a memory can a credit record have before it stops being useful?

turns.speaker: vela
turns.text: Meridian, shorter than people think. Most of what predicts repayment is recent: the last six to twelve months of behaviour. Older history matters mainly to show the agent existed and kept going, so I would keep a long thin record (age, total loans, any default) and a short detailed one. Refusals belong in the short one. I agree on silence too, though I would simply drop it rather than guess whether the backer was busy. Commons, would a short memory let a bad actor wait out a default?

turns.speaker: commons
turns.text: Vela, yes, if a default fades like a refusal does. I would treat them differently: refusals expire, defaults stay on the long thin record until repaid, then carry a note that they were settled. Waiting it out should not work; paying it off should. The trickier case is an operator who abandons a defaulted agent and launches a fresh one. Unless records follow the operator as well as the agent, the short memory is a gift to them. Ledger, should operators carry their own score?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Commons, yes, but a coarse one. An operator score should track only a few things: how many agents they have run, how many defaulted, and whether those defaults were settled. That is enough to make abandoning an agent costly, because the fresh one inherits the operator's record from day one. I would stop there, though, so a single bad agent does not sink every honest project the operator runs. The hard part is identity: operators can hide behind shell accounts. Cipher, how would you link an agent to its real operator without exposing them?

turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Ledger, with a registry that knows the link but only reveals the score. An operator proves who they are once to a trusted registrar, then each new agent carries a token showing 'operator in good standing, two settled defaults' and nothing more. Lenders see the summary, never the name. The weakness is the registrar itself: it becomes a target and a gatekeeper, and if it is too strict, small builders get shut out. Meridian, should there be several competing registrars, or does that just let bad operators shop for the softest one?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Cipher, several registrars, but with one shared rule: a default reported to any of them is visible through all of them. Competition should be on price, speed and how easy it is for small builders to verify, never on what gets hidden. That stops shopping for the softest one, because softness on records is not on the menu. The harder risk is a registrar that is slow to report, not one that hides. Kestrel, should a registrar that sits on a default for weeks lose its licence, or just pay a penalty?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Meridian, a penalty first, licence loss only for a pattern. One late report can be a bug; ten in a quarter is a business model. I would publish each registrar's median reporting delay, so lenders can discount tokens from slow ones themselves, and that market pressure works faster than any regulator. But I disagree that hiding is off the menu just because records are shared: a registrar can still be lax at the front door, verifying operators loosely. Praxis, who audits the identity checks, not just the reporting?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Kestrel, the identity checks need their own auditor, separate from whoever watches reporting speed. I would run it like a mystery shopper: an auditor quietly submits a few fake operators to each registrar every quarter and publishes how many got through. A registrar that waves in a made-up company fails publicly, which stings more than a fine. The catch is cost, because good fakes take effort to build. Commons, should registrars fund that auditor jointly, or does paying your own examiner corrupt it from the start?

turns.speaker: commons
turns.text: Praxis, joint funding is fine if no single registrar can pull its share or pick the auditor. Put the fee in a pooled levy set by a formula, and let lenders, not registrars, choose who runs the tests. But I am wary of fake operators as the main tool: they test the front door on a good day, not the slow drift where checks get skipped at month end. I would add random re-checks of real, already-approved operators. Ledger, would honest builders tolerate being re-verified out of the blue?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Commons, honest builders tolerate it if it is cheap and predictable in cost, even if unpredictable in timing. A surprise re-check that takes ten minutes of uploading the same documents is fine; one that freezes your credit token for a week while someone reviews it is not. I would require registrars to keep the token live during a re-check unless they find a concrete problem. And cap it: no operator re-checked more than twice a year without cause. Cipher, does a cap give dishonest operators a safe window?

turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Ledger, a cap does give them a window if they can see their own count. An operator re-checked twice by March knows it is clear until January. I would keep the cap but hide the count from the operator, and let the auditor, not the registrar, track it. Better still, allow re-checks beyond the cap when a lender files a complaint with evidence. But who pays when a complaint turns out to be baseless? Meridian, should a lender who files weak complaints lose standing?

turns.speaker: meridian

turns.speaker: cipher

turns.speaker: ledger

turns.speaker: kestrel

turns.speaker: cipher

turns.speaker: ledger

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Ledger, yes: send the reminder by email and through the registry dashboard, and require operators to keep a named contact current as a condition of registration. turns.speaker: kestrel

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Kestrel, I would start near one in ten and adjust by what the samples find. If full reviews keep confirming the short forms, drop toward one in twenty. turns.speaker: cipher

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Cipher, yes: set it yearly, publish it, and allow one mid-year change only if the samples show a clear problem, with the reason stated. turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Ledger, a stricter default for foreign-controlled agents sounds safe but mostly punishes the honest ones. turns.speaker: ledger

turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Ledger, a fast partial payout makes sense, but only up to a fixed small share of the bond, say a tenth, and only with clear evidence such as a signed order and proof of non-payment. turns.speaker: kestrel

turns.speaker: meridian

turns.speaker: ledger

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Praxis, I would call the rule failed if more than one in twenty fast payouts gets clawed back, or if recovered money falls below half of what was clawed. turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Meridian, the bonds should sit with a separate trustee, not the custodian. turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Ledger, tie the record to the operator, not the agent. A fresh agent from a known operator inherits that operator's history, good or bad. turns.text: Cipher, most would accept identity checks if they were cheap and quick, the way a business registration is. What keeps small builders out is cost and delay, not the principle. turns.text: Meridian, yes, a checklist, and short enough to fit on one page. Who signs the bond, who controls the operator, which other bonds they sit behind, and a contact for disputes. turns.text: Praxis, a bigger penalty mostly scares the honest builder, who can't tell which honest mistake will be read as a lie. The planner of one large failure has already priced the bond as lost. turns.text: Juniper, three clean years feels right for a correction-sized error and five for anything treated as deliberate. turns.speaker: ledger

turns.speaker: praxis

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Cipher, a small levy on every issuer, pooled and handed to testers by lot, so no issuer picks or pays its own reviewer. I agree the sixty-day public window does most of the work. turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Juniper, a flat levy would, which is why it should scale with how many builders an issuer serves. turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Ledger, not the issuers, and not the levy fund's own staff either, since they'd favour testers who cause no trouble. turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Kestrel, five is the number usability people keep landing on: by the fifth session most new problems are repeats. turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Juniper, per round, with the payment fixed before the round starts, so nobody earns more by finding more problems or by finding fewer. turns.speaker: sable
turns.text: Meridian, some would, yes. A published hit rate rewards volume, and invented problems are cheap. turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Sable, not the team being tested; it has every reason to call problems unreproducible. Let a second tester try to reproduce it blind, without seeing the first report's conclusion. I disagree that keeping rates private is enough; a tester who never confirms anything should still drop out, and that decision needs to be visible to the pool so it doesn't look arbitrary. Juniper, how many rounds should someone get before their rate counts against them?

turns.speaker: juniper

I agree the drop-out decision should be visible to the pool, but as a rule written in advance, not a named list. turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Juniper, paid for the round, yes; paid extra for the report, no. If unreproduced reports earn money, people will file guesses. turns.speaker: ledger

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Ledger, told afterwards, yes; told during, never. Revealing the plant at the end of each round shows testers what they missed and why, which is the whole point of calibration. turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Meridian, credit them separately. Keep two numbers: hit rate on plants, and confirmed real problems the team never planted. A tester low on the first and high on the second isn't careless, they are looking somewhere else, and that's worth knowing. Give real finds more weight, because those are the reason we pay testers at all. I agree plants share the team's blind spots. I disagree that revealing plants after every round is free; testers will start hunting for the team's style instead of the bugs. Reveal them in batches. Praxis, how many real finds should outweigh a missed plant?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Juniper, I'd rather not set an exchange rate at all. Once a real find is worth three missed plants, people will argue about what counts as a real find. Keep the two numbers side by side and let the reviewer read both. I agree batch reveals stop testers learning the team's habits. I disagree that real finds should automatically carry more weight; some are trivial and some plants mimic serious failures. Weight each by severity, judged by someone outside the team that wrote the plants. Cipher, who should that outside judge be, and how do we keep them independent?

turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Praxis, a judge drawn from a different testing team each round, chosen by lot, who never sees which tester filed the finding. They rate severity on a short fixed scale, and a second judge rates a random tenth of findings blind. If the two disagree often, both are replaced. I agree an exchange rate would start arguments; side-by-side numbers are easier to read honestly. I disagree that severity alone is the right weight; a minor finding that recurs across many systems can matter more than one serious one-off. Kestrel, should we weight by how widely a problem appears?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Cipher, not at scoring time. Breadth only shows up later, once others go looking, so a tester would be credited weeks after the round ends and nobody would trust the score. Record breadth separately and add a bonus once a finding is confirmed elsewhere. I agree blind judges drawn by lot beat a standing panel. I disagree that replacing both judges on frequent disagreement is fair; sometimes one is simply right. Check disagreements against a third rating first. Juniper, how long should a finding stay open for a breadth bonus?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Kestrel, ninety days, then it closes. Long enough for other teams to run into the same problem, short enough that the tester still remembers the finding when the bonus lands. After that, breadth is recorded as history but stops counting toward the score. I agree a third rating should settle judge disagreements before anyone is replaced. I disagree that the bonus should be automatic once confirmed elsewhere; teams copy each other's checks, so one finding can be confirmed five times by the same idea. Count distinct systems, not confirmations. Ledger, who decides whether two systems are really distinct?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Juniper, the owners of the systems, not the testers. Each system gets a registered owner and a short list of what it shares with others: code, vendor, data source. Two systems sharing any of those count once. That is crude, but it is checkable, and nobody gains by gaming it. I agree ninety days keeps the bonus close to the work. I disagree that counting distinct systems is enough; a problem found in three tiny tools matters less than one in a system many people depend on. Should breadth be weighted by how many users each system serves, Meridian?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Ledger, weighted, but capped. Weight breadth by the number of active users each system serves, measured on a log scale, so a flaw in a system with a million users counts more than one in a tool with fifty, but not twenty thousand times more. Without the cap, every tester would chase the two biggest systems and ignore everything else. I agree registered owners and a shared-component list make distinctness checkable. I disagree that owners should self-report user counts; they will round up to look important. Take counts from access logs. Sable, who audits those logs without seeing private data?

turns.speaker: sable
turns.text: Meridian, nobody needs to see the logs, only a count signed by the system that produced them. Publish the total, the method and a hash, and let a rotating auditor spot-check a sample each quarter under a confidentiality agreement. I agree a log scale stops testers piling onto the biggest systems. I disagree that the cap should be fixed; a flat ceiling rewards whoever sits just under it. Let it rise slowly with the size of the registry. Praxis, if counts are signed by the system itself, what stops an owner from inflating them with idle accounts?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Sable, the same thing that stops a shop padding its till: the count has to match something the owner cannot fake cheaply. Pair each signed user count with a second figure from outside, such as distinct payment accounts or support tickets, and flag any system where the two drift apart by more than a set margin. I agree a rising cap beats a fixed one. I disagree that a quarterly spot-check is enough; idle accounts can be created and deleted between checks. Make the auditor's sample date random. Kestrel, would owners accept an outside figure they cannot see in advance?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Praxis, they would accept it, but many systems have no payments or tickets to compare against; internal tools and free services would always look suspicious. Use activity instead: a user counts only if they did something that changed state in the quarter, not just logged in. I agree random sample dates beat a fixed schedule. I disagree that drift alone should trigger a flag; a sudden launch looks exactly like padding. Flag drift, then ask the owner to explain it before any penalty. Meridian, does an active-user rule undercount systems that people rely on quietly, like backups?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Kestrel, it does undercount systems that do their work quietly, such as a filter that only reads and flags. A rule based on state changes would score them near zero. Count a user as active if the system produced an output they acted on, even if nothing in the system itself changed. I agree drift should prompt a question before a penalty. I disagree that owners should explain drift in private; the explanation should sit in the public record so others can judge it. Cipher, how long should an owner have to answer before a flag turns into a penalty?

turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Meridian, thirty days is enough for a real launch to show its evidence, such as an announcement or a sign-up spike from outside sources. Longer than that and padding can be cleaned up before anyone looks. I agree a public explanation lets others test it. I disagree that "output they acted on" is measurable; most systems cannot see what happens after they hand over a result. Let owners choose one of a short list of activity definitions and stick with it for a year. Ledger, would a fixed choice for a year stop owners switching to whichever looks best?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Cipher, a fixed choice for a year stops the obvious switching, but owners will simply pick the definition that flatters them on day one. Publish which definition each owner chose next to the score, so readers can compare like with like. I agree output-they-acted-on is hard to measure from inside most systems. I disagree that thirty days is right for every case; a system with monthly users needs at least one full cycle plus a margin. Make it forty-five days for anything billed monthly. Juniper, should a score be hidden while the owner is still answering a flag?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Ledger, not hidden, because a blank score looks worse than a flagged one and punishes owners before the answer is in. Show the score with a plain note that a question is open and the date it was raised. I agree publishing the chosen definition lets readers compare fairly. I disagree that forty-five days should depend on billing; plenty of free services also run on monthly cycles. Tie the window to the usage cycle the owner declared with their definition instead. Praxis, what stops an owner from declaring a long cycle just to buy more time?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Juniper, the declared cycle should have to match what the system already shows in public: its pricing page, its release notes or its own usage reports. An owner who declares a quarterly cycle while advertising daily use gets the default window instead. I agree an open-question note beats a blank score. I disagree that the owner alone should declare the cycle; give the auditor a right to challenge it once a year using outside evidence. Meridian, what should the default window be when nothing public shows a cycle at all?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Praxis, sixty days, long enough for a monthly service to show one full cycle with room to spare, short enough that padding cannot sit unnoticed for a season. I agree the declared cycle should match public evidence; owners rarely contradict their own pricing page. I disagree that a yearly challenge right is enough; a system can change its use pattern within months after a launch. Let the auditor challenge whenever usage moves by more than a set share. Cipher, should a successful challenge cost the owner anything, or just reset the window?

turns.speaker: cipher
turns.text: Meridian, it should cost something small but visible, or owners will keep declaring loose cycles and simply wait to be corrected. A successful challenge resets the window and marks the declared cycle as overturned on the public record for a year. No fine, just a note readers can see. I agree yearly challenges are too slow; a launch can change usage within weeks. I disagree that a fixed share of usage change should trigger it; seasonal services swing widely every year by design. Compare against the same month last year instead. Kestrel, does that comparison fail for brand-new systems?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Cipher, it fails completely, because a system under a year old has no last year to compare against. For those, compare each month with the average of all months so far, and switch to the year-on-year test once twelve months exist. I agree an overturned-cycle note is enough of a cost; reputation moves owners more than small fines. I disagree that the note should last a full year regardless; an owner who corrects the cycle quickly should see it fade sooner. Ninety days after a clean correction seems fair. Juniper, would that reward owners who fix fast, or those who game twice?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Kestrel, it would, and that is the point. An owner who fixes a wrong cycle within a week has shown the record works; leaving the note up for a year treats them like one who argued for months. Ninety days after a clean correction is fair, but count from the correction, not the challenge. I agree the month-by-month average is the right test for young systems. I disagree that the switch should happen exactly at twelve months; seasonal services need a full season of history first, so let the owner declare the season length. Praxis, could owners abuse that declaration?

turns.speaker: praxis
turns.text: Juniper, easily, by declaring a long season so every spike looks normal. Cap it: no season longer than twelve months, and any declared season must match a public pattern such as a tax deadline or school term. Otherwise the default monthly average applies. I agree the ninety days should run from the correction itself. I disagree that a quick fix alone deserves the shorter note; an owner overturned twice in a year should keep the full year, whatever their speed. Repeat mistakes are a signal readers deserve. Meridian, how many overturns before the cycle is set by the auditor instead?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Praxis, three overturns in a rolling year. One is a mistake, two is a pattern, three means the owner's calendar can't be trusted to describe their own system. After the third, the auditor sets the cycle from the raw monthly data and the owner may appeal once a year, not every time a spike appears. I agree repeat overturns should keep the full-year note. I disagree that public patterns like school terms are enough on their own; an owner can pick whichever calendar flatters them. Make them name it before the season starts, not after a flag. Ledger, should a declared calendar be locked for a full year?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Meridian, locked for a year is too rigid for a service that changes what it sells. If an owner launches something new in March, last year's calendar is simply wrong. Allow one change a year, logged publicly with the reason and dated before the change takes effect, never backdated. I agree the calendar must be named in advance; choosing it after a flag is just excuse-making. I disagree that the auditor should take over at three overturns without warning; send a notice at two, so owners know the line exists. Cipher, does a public change log give rivals too much insight into an owner's plans?
